# /continuity-review

## Purpose

Check that the issue holds together from its first page to its last, and
that it connects to the issue before it. Page reviews look at one page and
its two neighbors. This command reads the whole run: the ledger in story
order, the reviewed renders side by side at every page boundary, and each
character and object from first appearance to last. It ends by writing the
state the issue leaves behind, which is where the next issue starts.

## Use When

- Every page of an issue has a reviewed render, before `/build-edition`.
- A page was repaired late. A page repaired last can still break the page
  after it.
- A bible or a master was versioned after pages were rendered.
- A new issue is about to be planned and needs the state it opens from.

## Inputs

- `issue` (ID, required): the `ISS_###` to audit.
- `scope` (enum, optional, default `full`): `ledger` (plan only) | `renders`
  (pixels at page boundaries) | `boundary` (the join with the previous
  issue) | `full`.
- `--check` (flag, optional): report only; write no state file and add no
  findings.

## Invokes Agents

- continuity-editor
- production-qa

## Required Skills

- continuity-checking
- state-tracking

## Process

1. Load the pages in page-number order, whatever order they were generated
   or repaired in, with their ledgers, current renders, and review files.
   If `issue.yaml` has `opens_from`, load that final-state file.
2. Run the mechanical audit: `node scripts/check-continuity.js --root
   production --issue <ISS_ID>`. Send every error back to `/panel-ledger`
   and run again until none remain. Decide each warning: fix it, or record
   why it stands.
3. Check the opening boundary. Compare the incoming state with the first
   appearance of each character and prop: location, position, wardrobe,
   state tags, and what is held. A difference needs a cause the reader is
   given: a scene transition, an `ellipsis`, a `wardrobe_change`, or a
   `transfers` entry. Then open the last reviewed page of the previous
   issue beside the first page of this one and compare the pixels.
4. Audit what the script cannot judge in the plan. Within each scene the
   map's side convention holds in every panel, travel and threat keep the
   directions in `geography`, and time of day and wardrobe agree with the
   story bible's timeline between scenes.
5. Audit the page boundaries on reviewed renders. Open each page beside the
   next and compare the last panel of one with the first of the other: the
   same person, the same outfit, the same injuries, the same object with
   the same shape in the same hand, landmarks on the same side.
6. Look along the whole issue for slow drift that no single boundary
   shows. Compare the first and last appearance of each character and of
   each plot-relevant prop.
7. Record each visual defect as a finding in the review file of the page
   that shows it, under the matching check, with `expected`, `visible`,
   `severity`, and `repair`. A blocking finding changes that review's
   verdict to `flagged`, returns the page to `rendered`, and sends it to
   `/repair-page`. A defect in the plan goes to `/panel-ledger`.
8. Write `production/continuity/<ISS_ID>.final-state.yaml`: `issue`,
   `after_page`, and under `characters` the `location`, `position`,
   `wardrobe`, `state`, and `holding` of each one from their last ledger
   row, off-panel rows included. Under `props`, the `custody`, `location`,
   and `state` of each tracked object. List the `open_threads` the next
   issue has to pick up.
9. Check the state file against the pixels of the last page. Where the
   render that will ship differs from the ledger, the next issue inherits
   what readers saw. Repair the page, or record the difference in
   `open_issues` with a `severity`, the `page`, and a `description`.
10. production-qa confirms the gates: every page has a `current_render`
    whose review is `pass` or `fixed`, no review exceeds the repair limit,
    and `node scripts/validate-workspace.js --root production --issue
    <ISS_ID>` passes. Set `last_validated`, and set the issue's `status`
    to `review`.
11. Run the self-evaluation gates on the state file and report in two
    parts that are never folded together: the script result (errors and
    warnings by count and code) and the visual findings (by page and
    check).

## Outputs

- `production/continuity/<ISS_ID>.final-state.yaml`, validates against
  `schemas/continuity-state.schema.json`.
- New findings in
  `production/issues/<ISS_ID>/pages/<PG_ID>/reviews/<RENDER_ID>.review.yaml`
  (`schemas/visual-review.schema.json`), where a boundary exposed a defect.
- `production/issues/<ISS_ID>/issue.yaml`, `status` updated
  (`schemas/issue.schema.json`).

## Notes

- This command generates nothing and costs nothing. Run it as often as you
  like.
- An entry in `open_issues` with `severity: blocking` keeps the edition a
  draft. Clear it, or get the user's decision, before `/build-edition`
  builds anything else.
- The next issue's `issue.yaml` points at this state file through
  `opens_from`, and `/panel-ledger` starts its first rows from it.
- Fix a defect at the cheapest layer that owns it. A missing transfer is a
  plan fix. A wrong face on one page is a repair. Neither is solved by a
  caption.
- Format differences: in a webtoon the boundary between two segments is
  seen in one scroll, with no page turn to hide a jump, so compare segment
  joins at reading size.
- Related: `/visual-review` (page by page), `/repair-page` (findings from
  this audit), `/panel-ledger` (plan errors), `/build-edition` (gated by
  this), `/issue-breakdown` (the next issue reads the state).
